output.brief: The enrolment drop is mainly a yield problem, not an applicant problem. Applications, admits and GPA all rose. Yield fell only in the tiers where the new merit schedule cut award amounts: Dean's awards fell from $14,000 to $9,000 and yield from 45.2% to 31.9%, and Merit awards fell from $9,000 to $5,000 and yield from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and their yield held at about 36%, and the no-award group held at about 37%. Early-action yield also fell by about 7 points, even though those decisions went out on time on the old system. So slow regular-decision turnaround cannot be the main cause, though it may have cost a few students. I'm fairly confident, but the data doesn't separate price effects from other causes within each tier. Next steps: don't replace the Admissions director on this evidence. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers before the next award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decisions. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claim is checked.
output.methodChoice: Collected X13 (yield by scholarship tier) and X3 (yield by admission round) to separate the price explanation from the turnaround explanation.
